question: Latter-day Saint scripture distinguishes 'spirit' from ordinary matter. Which statement best captures the doctrine taught in D&C 131?
choices: There is no such thing as immaterial matter; all spirit is matter, but finer and purer, discernible only to purified eyes
Spirit is immaterial and wholly unlike physical matter, which is why God can be a spirit without a body
Spirit is created out of nothing and will one day be dissolved back into nothing at the final judgment
Spirit and matter are two eternal opposites that can never be joined, so resurrection unites a body with a separate, alien substance
notes: A is correct (D&C 131:7-8). B is the classic immaterial-spirit dualism of creedal Christianity (protestant_trap). C smuggles in ex nihilo and annihilation (protestant_trap). D is a Manichaean-style spirit/matter dualism sometimes assumed by members (folk_doctrine_trap). Tests LDS materialism: spirit is a refined form of matter, which underlies embodiment of God and a literal resurrection.

question: In 2 Nephi 2, Lehi argues that agency itself depends on a prior condition. Which condition does he say must exist for there to be real moral agency?
choices: A written law revealed by prophets, without which no choice has moral weight
A perfected conscience given at birth that infallibly knows right from wrong
Opposition in all things — a real enticement to good and to evil, with both available to choose
A neutral will untouched by any inclination, so that every choice is perfectly uncaused
notes: A confuses accountability-under-law with the precondition of agency itself (plausible_near_miss). B is a folk overstatement of an infallible inborn conscience (folk_doctrine_trap). C is correct. D imports a libertarian 'liberty of indifference' philosophy alien to the text (progressive_trap). Tests Lehi's argument that without opposition (a thing to act and a thing to be acted upon) there is no agency, no good, no purpose in creation.

question: King Benjamin (Mosiah 3) and Abinadi (Mosiah 15) both teach about the Atonement. Which statement best reflects their combined doctrine on how Christ redeems and why?
choices: Christ's death merely sets a moral example; redemption comes from following that example, not from any vicarious payment
Because the Atonement is infinite, all mankind are unconditionally saved in the celestial kingdom regardless of repentance
Christ atoned only for original sin inherited from Adam; individual sins must be paid for by the sinner's own suffering
The atoning blood of Christ redeems those who fall by transgression and were ignorant of the law, and saves the rest conditioned on repentance and faith on His name
notes: A is the moral-influence-only theory (progressive_trap). B is universalism that erases repentance (progressive_trap). C mixes original-sin satisfaction with self-atonement, both contrary to LDS doctrine (protestant_trap). D is correct. Tests Benjamin/Abinadi: the Atonement covers the ignorant and those who die in infancy unconditionally, while the accountable are saved conditioned on repentance and faith — not blanket universalism, not example-only.

question: Abraham 3 describes the premortal estate and the choosing of leaders. Which statement most accurately reflects the doctrine of foreordination it teaches?
choices: The noble and great ones were unconditionally predestined to be saved, and the rest to be lost, before they were born
Certain spirits were foreordained to specific missions and callings, but foreordination does not override mortal agency or guarantee exaltation
All spirits were created equal in every capacity, so any apparent foreordination is merely God foreseeing random outcomes
Foreordination means God merely guessed who might do well, since even He could not know the future of free agents
notes: A is Calvinist double predestination (protestant_trap). C flattens premortal differences and denies real foreordination (correlation_oversimplification). D is open-theism denying God's foreknowledge (progressive_trap). Tests the distinction LDS doctrine draws between foreordination (a call to a mission, still requiring faithful agency) and predestination (a guaranteed, unconditional outcome).

question: Sons of perdition are the only ones excluded from any degree of glory. According to D&C 76, what does a person have to do to become a son of perdition?
choices: Having received a sure witness of the Son by the Holy Ghost, then deny that witness and crucify Christ to themselves, putting Him to open shame
Commit any unrepented serious sin, such as murder or adultery, and die without forgiveness
Simply reject the gospel during mortality, even without ever having known its truth
Be born under a curse foreordained in the premortal world with no possibility of repentance
notes: A is correct. B treats grave sin as automatically damning to perdition (correlation_oversimplification) — such sins, unrepented, lead to telestial glory, not perdition. C lowers the bar to mere rejection (plausible_near_miss). D imports a premortal-curse fatalism (folk_doctrine_trap). Tests D&C 76: perdition requires having received the sure witness, then defiantly denying it — the unpardonable sin, not ordinary serious sin.

question: How does Latter-day Saint doctrine, drawing on Moroni 8 and the 2nd Article of Faith, treat the standing of little children before God?
choices: Children inherit Adam's guilt and need infant baptism to be cleansed of original sin
Children are morally neutral and earn their own salvation gradually as they perform good works
Children are saved through Christ's Atonement and are not capable of sin until the age of accountability; infant baptism is a solemn mockery
Children are unconditionally saved only if their parents are temple-worthy members
notes: A is the original-sin/infant-baptism doctrine (protestant_trap). B is a Pelagian works-earning view (progressive_trap). C is correct. D makes a child's salvation depend on parental worthiness, a folk distortion (folk_doctrine_trap). Tests Mormon's epistle: little children are whole and alive in Christ, baptism before accountability (age 8) is unnecessary and a mockery, and men are punished only for their own sins.

question: Moses 7 describes Enoch's city of Zion. Which statement best reflects the doctrine the chapter teaches about Zion?
choices: Zion is purely a future heavenly reward and was never meant to be built on the earth
Zion refers only to the physical city of Jerusalem, which will be rebuilt in the last days
Zion is a state of private inner peace that has nothing to do with a community or society
The people of Zion were of one heart and one mind, dwelt in righteousness with no poor among them, and the city was taken up to God
notes: A spiritualizes Zion away from earth as a purely future reward (progressive_trap). B restricts Zion to old Jerusalem, ignoring the LDS dual-Zion concept and Enoch's city (plausible_near_miss). C individualizes it into mere private inner peace (progressive_trap). D is correct. Tests Moses 7:18 — Zion as a unified, righteous community with no poor, the pattern the latter-day Church is to build, and the translated city of Enoch.

question: The Restoration involved priesthood being conferred by resurrected and translated messengers. Which sequence and source correctly matches the keys restored?
choices: The Aaronic Priesthood was conferred by John the Baptist, and the Melchizedek Priesthood by Peter, James, and John
The Melchizedek Priesthood came first, conferred by Moses, followed by the Aaronic Priesthood from Elijah
Both priesthoods were conferred at once by the angel Moroni when he delivered the plates
Joseph Smith ordained himself to both priesthoods by revelation, without any heavenly messenger
notes: A is correct. B swaps the messengers and order — Moses and Elijah restored other keys later at Kirtland (D&C 110), not the priesthoods themselves (plausible_near_miss). C attributes the conferral to Moroni (plausible_near_miss). D is the hostile 'he invented it himself' claim (anti_mormon_trap). Tests the specific restoration sequence: John the Baptist (Aaronic, May 1829), then Peter, James, and John (Melchizedek).

question: In the Book of Mormon, Alma 32 develops a doctrine of faith. Which statement best captures how Alma defines and tests faith?
choices: Faith is a firm belief held with absolute certainty, and any doubt proves a lack of faith
Faith is mere intellectual assent to correct propositions, separate from any action or experiment
Faith is not a perfect knowledge but a hope in things not seen which are true; it is tested by experiment, planting the word and observing whether it enlarges the soul
Faith is a feeling of peace that requires no evidence and cannot be examined or tested in any way
notes: A equates faith with certainty and demonizes doubt (correlation_oversimplification). B is a dead intellectual-assent faith divorced from works (protestant_trap, contra James 2). C is correct. D makes faith unfalsifiable and unexaminable (progressive_trap). Tests Alma 32: faith as hope in unseen truths, an active experiment on the word that grows by its fruits — neither blind certainty nor passive assent.
